extracted.intended_audience: writers, literature students, and educators interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Describe, analyze, or create character foils: characters (or plots/subplots) that contrast with other characters (typically the protagonist) to highlight or differentiate qualities, choices, or outcomes. Guidance covers types of foil, dimensions of contrast, and literary examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition of a foil
rubrics_metrics.description: In any narrative, a foil is a character who contrasts with another character, typically, a character who contrasts with the protagonist, in order to better highlight or differentiate certain qualities of the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a foil to make traits of the protagonist more visible by juxtaposition. The page frames this as the central purpose of a foil and provides multiple literary examples (e.g., Don Quixote and Sancho Panza). The definition implies the foil's role is comparative rather than merely secondary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foil may be the antagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: A foil to the protagonist may also be the antagonist of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing foils, consider making the antagonist functionally serve as a foil so that conflict also illuminates protagonist traits (example implication: many classic dramas have antagonists who highlight protagonists' values). This is explicitly noted as a common relationship between foil and antagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot or 'story within a story' as a foil
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, a subplot can be used as a foil to the main plot. This is especially true in the case of metafiction and the 'story within a story' motif.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foiling need not be limited to individual characters — contrast can be enacted between plotlines to reveal thematic or moral differences. Use parallel or contrapuntal subplots to set off the main plot's choices or outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foil by dramatic or extreme comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: A foil usually either differs dramatically or is an extreme comparison that is made to contrast a difference between two things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create stark oppositions (e.g., temperament, values, abilities) rather than subtle variation when the aim is to sharply illuminate differences. The page highlights that extreme or dramatic contrast is a common technique for effective foils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gieryn's three categories of foil use
rubrics_metrics.description: Thomas F. Gieryn's taxonomy (explained via Tamara A. P. Metze) groups foil uses into three categories: those that emphasize the heightened contrast (this is different because ...), those that operate by exclusion (this is not X because...), and those that assign blame ('due to the slow decision-making procedures of government...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or creating foils, consider which rhetorical operation you want: (1) heightened contrast to spotlight difference; (2) exclusion to define identity by negation; (3) assigning blame to redirect critique or causal responsibility. Examples in critical theory can guide which category best suits your narrative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foils can contrast across multiple dimensions (appearance, wealth, morals, choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foils are often constructed by juxtaposing differences in looks, social position, inheritance, morals, intelligence, or choices (e.g., Edgar Linton vs. Heathcliff: looks, money, inheritance, morals; Lennie vs. George: size/strength vs. intellect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select one or several axes of difference (physical, socioeconomic, moral, intellectual, behavioral) to produce meaningful contrast. Use concrete particulars (appearance, inheritance, moral choices) to make contrasts vivid for readers. The page gives numerous literary examples demonstrating this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foil as a comedic device / 'straight man'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'straight man' is a form of foil in comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comedic contexts, the straight man provides a foil by reacting with seriousness or normalcy to highlight the comic character's oddities. When writing comedy, consider timing and reaction beats: the straight man's normalcy amplifies the humor of the comic foil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foils can be signalled explicitly in text (word play / dialogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters may explicitly acknowledge or enact foiling (example: Hamlet tells Laertes 'I'll be your foil' in Act V Scene 2), revealing the foil relationship via word play or direct reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can use dialogue, meta-commentary, or word play to mark or reinforce a foil relationship. Explicit acknowledgement can be a stylistic choice to draw readers' attention to the comparative function being played out.
